utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-02-55-Misc.6, the Macedonian Deferral Case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. To begin with, may we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Office of the Prosecutor is represented -- it's not the accusation here, but I'm here with Mr. Alex Whiting, who is a trial attorney. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now may I turn to the representative of the former Yugoslavia Republic of Macedonia. Would you please turn yourself and your team to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. I did not get the translation. Would you please try it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry again, you know. It seems to be there is some technical problem, you know. We did not get the translation because the language of Macedonian is something new in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me in English now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the English language be heard now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It will be more complicated for us, but I believe we can continue like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Stavre Djikov I am the Public Prosecutor General for the Republic of Macedonia. My deputies and assistants are Maja Koneska and Marko Zvrlevski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This hearing, pursuant to the decision rendered by this Trial Chamber on September 10th, 2002, under motion of request for deferral of certain investigations and the proceedings in the Republic of Macedonia. On September 5th, 2002, the Prosecutor filed a motion to President to assign a Trial Chamber to Prosecutor's defence deferral request. By the order of the president assigned a case to the Chamber dated September 6th, 2002, the case was assigned to Trial Chamber I. The Trial Chamber received the Prosecutor's request for deferral and a motion for order to the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia dated September 5th, 2002. On September 10, 2002, Trial Chamber I held an informal hearing of the Office of the Prosecutor on the motion, and on the same day, this Trial Chamber made a decision rejecting Prosecutor's request for an interim order from the Trial Chamber to stop the commencement of a criminal proceeding on the next day in the Republic of Macedonia. The key issue of this hearing is about the request for overall deferral of any future --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- and the proceedings in the Republic of Macedonia. Since the Prosecution made the application, I would like to ask the Prosecutor to present her case first. Then we will turn to the representative of the Republic of Macedonia. If any party believes that certain parts of the representation will jeopardise the ongoing investigations or proceedings or disclose any state secret, please feel free to ask this Trial Chamber for private session during the hearing. Now, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'm appearing today because I've had -- I've been in charge of contact with the authorities of Macedonia for the ongoing investigation and also for the questions of deferral and primacy of the Tribunal. In 2001 already, last year, international organisations that were present in Macedonia drew our attention to the fact that crimes coming under our jurisdiction were being committed on the territory of Macedonia. I'm talking, of course, of organisations such as the European Union, the United Nations, and especially NATO. In our motion, in our written motion, you will have a letter from the president of Macedonia, dated October 2001 and it was raising the same issue. Following that, we decided based on the first elements that were communicated to us, we decided to open two investigations. One investigation called Neprosteno and the other one called Ljuboten. I would like to stress today that what we learned, what we saw about what was going on in Macedonia was the beginning of a sort of repetition of crimes that had already been seen in other countries, in Bosnia and in Serbia, and it was obvious that these were crimes that came under our jurisdiction. At the same time, the Macedonian authorities started new investigations, and we exchanged information. The Macedonian authorities were sending us information, and it was quite obvious that the facts of these crimes, these other crimes, were related to the ongoing investigation at our office, and thus at the beginning of the year, we realised that it was vital for us to invoke primacy, the primacy of the Tribunal, for the various reasons that are laid out in our written motion. As a rule, because it's not the first time that we are faced with such an issue, so I should say that as a rule, when we are talking about investigations, it's usually enough to inform the national authorities and the country involved, and our primacy is usually accepted immediately. We went to Skopje in Macedonia in order to discuss the matter of the primacy of the Tribunal, and the general prosecutor, who is here with us today, will be in a position to confirm that there weren't any problems in that respect. The judicial authority in the person of the prosecutor was agreeable and agreed to recognise the primacy of the Tribunal. Later on, this position changed, this opinion changed, because according to the High Court, it seems necessary to the Macedonian authorities to now ask for a formal, for an official decision rendered by a Trial Chamber of the Tribunal. So here we are faced with different interpretations. I discussed the matter with the President of the Tribunal, and he agreed with our interpretation, an interpretation that is not as restrictive as the interpretation of the Macedonian authorities, and I informed the prosecutor in Skopje about that, but apparently we are still in the same position. We are still here discussing about formality. We are here because an official decision for deferral has been asked by the Macedonian government in favour of the Tribunal. Therefore, we are here talking about the implementation of Rule 9 and Rule 10 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I am not going to repeat what is in the written motion, but, Your Honours, I will give a brief summary of the conditions that are necessary for a formal request for deferral to be granted. The Prosecutor must prove that an investigation is currently being conducted by the Prosecutor on crimes that -- for which the Tribunal is competent and crimes that were committed in Macedonia in 2001. If necessary, I will let the Prosecutor for Macedonia -- will let him talk about the facts, but as far as we are concerned, there is no problem, there is no issue here. Second condition to be fulfilled, the facts investigated by the Prosecutor have to have been the subject of a procedure or investigation in the Republic of Macedonia, and that's the case. That's precisely the case. We should outline here that we are not only talking about criminal proceedings but about an investigation. So these acts are subject of investigations and proceedings. In this specific case, we are talking about an investigation, about investigations. The third condition to be fulfilled is that the subject of those national investigations have to be closely related to or otherwise involve significant factual or legal questions which may have implications for investigations of the Prosecutor. In paragraphs 13 and 14, we list these facts, and I would like to add another one. In Macedonian law, the protection of witnesses is not provided for. It's not provided for in Macedonian law. But that's absolutely vital, essential, for these investigations to be successful. Therefore, together with the other reasons already stated, the fact that here we have things that are closely related to our investigation, the fact -- it's not very important to stress that there's no witness protection provided for. Another element I'd like to add is the law of amnesty. You know that in Macedonia a law has been voted for the crimes committed in 2001, and under Article 1 of the law, it is stated, very clearly, that the law on amnesty does not cover crimes that come under the jurisdiction of The Hague Tribunal. That means that any investigation on crimes against humanity, crimes of genocide, war crimes, any of these crimes are not covered by the law of amnesty, but these crimes have to be subject to -- of proceedings or investigations by our Tribunal. I would like to add another remark. We are currently at the investigation stage. We do not know yet what will be the final outcome of the investigations, but I should like to stress that this is not a condition provided for by Rule 9 or by Rule 10 to grant deferral. The mandate given to us by the Security Council deals with people in high positions who committed crimes. But we have to start with the crimes committed on the smallest levels to then go up the ladder. Currently we cannot answer that question, because those who were accountable at the lowest levels, the lowest echelons, will not be dealt with here in the Tribunal. But what is important is that at the end of the investigations, the national authority will be able to deal with these smaller criminals if it deems necessary. I would like to remind you of the case-law of the Tribunal when it comes to deferrals. I'm familiar with two decisions, but I'd like to mention one, one issued on the 11th of May, 1995, a deferral related to Bosnia-Herzegovina. That refers to a decision of the 8th of November, 1994, in the Tadic case. The number of the Bosnia-Herzegovina case is IT-95-6D of the 11th of May, 1995. Thus, Your Honours, I believe that the deferral of investigations requested in our motion is adequate. If you look at Rule 9 and Rule 10 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. But this does not imply what will be the outcome of these investigations. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I now turn to the representative of the Republic of Macedonia. Sir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We thank you that with your decision upon case number IT-02-55 Misc. 6 dated, 10th September 2002, you have enabled the representative of Republic of Macedonia to present before the International Tribunal those wrongdoings that bear elements of criminal acts and elements of crimes against humanity which are codified by the criminal code of the Republic of Macedonia and also by your Statute and the relevant Rules of Procedure and Evidence and person operators of these crimes should be brought to justice before this international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to interrupt you. As I said before that your language is something new in this Tribunal. We have to rely on the relay of the translation, especially in the French channel. So could I kindly ask you to slow down and make a pause between each sentence. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the beginning, I would like to express my gratitude and the gratitude of the Macedonian nation and the representatives of the ethnic communities in Macedonia, Albanians, Turks, Serbs, Vlachs, Romas, Bosnians, and other ethnic groups in the Republic of Macedonia. Before I begin to elaborate the criminal and legal problem and the crisis in Republic of Macedonia, I would like to stress that in all contacts and work meetings that we had with the respected colleague the Prosecutor Ms. Carla Del Ponte and her deputy, Mr. Graham Blewitt, in our country, as well as in The Hague, we were all led in these meetings by the same goal, and that is the goal of justice and fairness --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- nor by the international community, and to protect the victims that have been -- over whom the cruel deaths, rape and arson, destruction of property and homes and with that to preventively prevent the future wrongdoing acts of the criminal gangs that do not recognise borders and whose only motive is to destroy the human lives, to humiliate the human dignity of the ordinary citizens, and to profit from the death and the other wrongdoings, gaining financial and political power with which they would control not only the freedom and the rights of the citizens and their life, but also to rule with the country. Honoured Judges, the Republic of Macedonia, since its independence in 1991, as an independent and sovereign state and a member of the organisation of the United Nations, has taken and fulfilled all its international obligations, especially the ones established by the international conventions and other documents. The constitution of our country, in Article 8, line 11, categorically and undoubtably stipulates that the generally accepted norms of the international law should be obeyed. In 1993, the assembly of the Republic of Macedonia passed very important decisions regarding its international obligations, among which the decision on accession to the international legal documents for the basic human rights and freedoms adopted by the organisation of the United Nations, which is -- which regards to the universal declaration on human rights of 1948. The international covenant on civil and political rights of 1966; the convention on prevention and punishment of crimes; genocide of 1948; the convention for non-application of the statute of limitations and crimes against humanity and other documents of 1968; and the decision for acceding to the Geneva Conventions and protocols for humanisation of war of 1949; the convention for protection of human rights and basic freedoms of 1953, by the Council of Europe. On the plan of the penal legislation, the obligations taken by these conventions for incrimination of certain hard crimes, severe crimes such as genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity are fulfilled with their introduction in the criminal law of Republic of Macedonia of 1996. The Republic of Macedonia strongly supports the process of development of the international penal law as supreme international law and of constitution and operation of the system of the international penal criminal justice, initiated in the Second World War with the Nuremberg Tribunal. Such a development expresses the determination of each individual that the existence of such system is the most secure guarantee for protection of the human freedoms and rights and that the existence of an efficient system of the international penal jurisdiction is the best preventive measure for prevention of the international crimes, for which nobody acts such preventively [As interpreted] as the knowledge that every perpetrator of such a crime will be brought before the face of justice, if not before the national, then before the international penal Tribunal. Such destiny, unfortunately, the Republic of Macedonia, without being involved in the military crashes, has undergone at the time of the disintegration of former Yugoslavia. A large number of its citizens were victims of the crimes perpetrated in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. On its territory, shelter was found by tens of thousands of refugees from the other former Yugoslav republics. Macedonia and its economy suffered great damage from the economic embargo against FRY, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the blockade or blockage of its frontiers or borders. During the Kosovo crisis in 1999, the Republic of Macedonia secured or accepted over 350.000 refugees, most of them ethnic Albanians, and a minority of them Serbs and Romas from Kosovo. Nevertheless, all these consequences of crimes committed in its neighbouring countries are minor and of no importance when compared to the impact that the Republic of Macedonia suffered from the criminal wave of violence which spread into the Balkans from Kosovo. The Republic of Macedonia and its citizens, regardless of their nationality, became victims of terrorist attacks of Albanian paramilitary formations which, in their attacks, which lasted for several months, carried out a series of international crimes: Genocide and forced deportation of the non-Albanian population from the area of the northwestern part of Macedonia; crimes against humanity, which were directed against the civilian population; war crimes and destruction of valuable cultural and historic monuments. These are the reasons that a serious interest by the Republic of Macedonia in the development of the system of the international penal law. Therefore, the Republic of Macedonia supported the work of The Hague Tribunal in convicting war crimes in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. In 1999, during the Kosovo crisis, the office of the ICTY was opened in Skopje, and ever since, intensive cooperation began between the state organs, the police, the Prosecution and courts, and the office of the ICTY. In the armed conflict that began in the night between 21st and 22nd of January, 2001, and initiated by the terrorist and criminal gang, the so-called National Liberation Army, the NLA, of Albanians from the Republic of Macedonia and the Kosovo protectorate which is part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. From those who organised, led, instigated, and other bodies and actors of the NLA, criminal acts were committed, as described in Article 2, Article 3, Article 5, and Article 7 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague, and prescribed and sanctioned in chapter 34, titled "Criminal Acts Against Humanity and the International Law in the Criminal Statute of the Republic of Macedonia." As a consequence to the activities of the terrorist gang, the so-called National Liberation Army, the NLA, whose ideological leaders were Fazli Veliu, Ali Ahmeti and Gzim Ostreni, and during the armed conflict in the Republic of Macedonia, in the period between January 2001 and 26th of September, 2001, until now, 82 members of the Macedonian security forces and 16 citizens have been killed. Out of these 16 civilians, 2 were members of the OSCE. About 300 policemen obtained bodily injuries, and so did members of the army and a large number of citizens, in a brutal manner and by applying force, and premeditated killings, ethnic cleansing has been carried out of the territory which was inhabited by ethnic Macedonians. From their own homes, more than 86.000 were displaced, and 80.000 citizens temporarily abandoned the Republic of Macedonia and stayed abroad. More than 40 religious buildings were damaged, including churches and mosques, of a great historical and cultural value. 92 persons were kidnapped, 20 persons are accounted missing, out of which 6 are ethnic Albanians, 13 are ethnic Macedonians, and one is a citizen of Bulgaria. Damage has been caused to the economy and to the citizens, which reaches the figure of around 1 billion Euros. Under a temporary occupation was and is, up to this date, 20 per cent of the territory in the northwestern parts of the state, which endangers the territorial integrity, the constitutional order, and the security of the Republic of Macedonia. Ministry of Interior to the competent public prosecutions in the Republic has lodged 75 criminal complaints against 245 suspects, members of the so-called National Liberation Army, for crimes committed against the state, from chapter 28, and crimes against humanity and the international law, from chapter 34, from the Criminal Code of the Republic of Macedonia. The law on amnesty, adopted on March 8, 2002, by the parliament of the Republic of Macedonia, and the Act on Pardon by the president of the state, as specific state legal enactments that represent political decision on the reduction of crisis and establishment of peace in the country. Excluded are from prosecution all the reported persons, except for 46 people -- 56 persons who are perpetrators of severe violations of the international humanitarian law. On these 56 persons, there are proceedings instigated before our courts, and lodged are proposals for prosecution against them to The Hague Tribunal. Respected Judges, Honourable Judges, the Republic of Macedonia has faced the most serious threats to its serenity and integrity, caused by an open aggression by organised and armed Albanian criminal terrorist gangs, led by the Albanian narc [phoen] mafia and armed war profiteers who came from Kosovo, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who called themselves NLA. The Public Prosecutor of the Republic of Macedonia, Senior Public Prosecutor, and the Basic Public Prosecutors, in accordance with their constitutional function of criminal prosecution of perpetrators of criminal acts, among which are the evil-doing acts of severe criminal offences and violations of the international humanitarian law on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia, and according also to the international rules and regulations, undertook activities for collection of evidence against the organisers, leaders, conspirers, and other perpetrators. Before the competent Macedonia courts ongoing are the procedures. Case 1: NLA leadership. Acting upon the criminal petition lodged by the Minister of Interior of the Republic of Macedonia, the Basic Public Prosecutor in Skopje, on July 30th, 2001, under KO number 2687/2001, has submitted a motion to the investigating judge within the Basic Court Skopje 2, a motion to conduct an investigation with a proposal to sentence a detention measure against Fazli Veliu, Ali Ahmeti, Gzim Ostreni, Musa Demiri, Daut Haradinaj, Shefit Djaferi, Mustafa Rustemi, Djavit Asan, Hisni Shakiri, Musa Djaferi and Djevat Ademi, due to the existence of basic suspicion that all of the aforementioned people, accused persons, have committed a crime punishing for the most severe forms of criminal enactments, according to the Article 327, paragraph 1, of the Criminal Code, and related to the criminal acts endangering of the territorial unity according to the Article 307, paragraph 1, armed rebellion under Article 312, paragraph 2; terrorism, under Article 313; and diversion, according to the Article 314; and all related to the Article 22 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Instead of "diversion," it should be "sabotage".

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now continuing. And the accused Ali Ahmeti, Fazli Veliu, and Gzim Ostreni have perpetrated a criminal act, genocide, under Article 403 from the Criminal Code; Criminal act war crime against prisoners of war, under Article 406 from the Criminal Code, and the criminal act war crime against the civilian population, under Article 404, paragraph 1, from the Criminal Code. The investigative judge before the competent court, with the decision KI number 413/01, of August 7th, 2001, decided to conduct an investigation against all defendants and has sentenced them to a detention measure calculated from the moment of their deprivation of liberty. In the subsequent period, on September 5th, 8th of October, and November 1st, and 7th of December, 2001, to the competent court were lodged three subsequent motions for extension of the investigation against the same perpetrators. The accused Fazli Veliu, Ali Ahmeti, Gzim Ostreni, Shefit Djaferi, Musa Djaferi, and Djevat Ademi from the Republic of Macedonia, as ideological organisers in 1999, have created a criminal terrorist organisation, a gang, the so-called National Liberation Army, NLA, with the headquarters, political and military wing, and five brigades, with a programme that has as its objective to unite in one state, within one state, all the territories where Albanians live, through organisation of an armed rebellion and perpetration of terrorist acts, to take away a part of the territory of the Republic of Macedonia in a way that the accused Fazli Veliu, as an ideological leader, advocates its ideas and is an ideological leader for military activities and its transformation from the liberation army of Kosovo into the National Liberation Army, NLA. The defendant Ali Ahmeti advocates in defence the aims of the NLA in communication with the national and the foreign public, giving statements and interviews for the media, in which he describes the military activities undertaken on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Until now, I realise that your statement is extremely long, and would you please, you know, summarise the main points in your statement in this courtroom, and you are allowed to submit that document to this Trial Chamber after the hearing. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dear President, Honourable Judges of the Tribunal, I will only go to the proposals that I would like to submit to this respected Court, and also I will communicate to you, submit the entire documentation. I will now present the proposal of the Macedonian authorities. Due to the previously stated facts, on behalf of the innocent victims, the law and the justice, I address you with the following proposals: I propose that The Hague Tribunal defers the legal jurisdiction over the three cases: NLA leadership, Mavrovo workers, and Lipkovo water supply, water reserve, where the suspects have been identified and on whom of Public Prosecutor of the Republic of Macedonia, upon the motion FSK number 98/02 of January 29th, 2002, to the office of the Chief Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal, Ms. Carla Del Ponte, has communicated proposals for prosecution an exhaustive court evidence materials. Macedonia competent courts and the Public Prosecutor have, with full professionality and in a timely manner, in circumstances unwarranted by the government bodies in the state, and neither by the citizens provoked armed conflict, and after the completion of the absurd conflict, impartially, independently, and diligently, in the past period, have conducted the investigative procedures, and as a result of it, firm evidence was collected that were communicated to the Prosecution of The Hague Tribunal. Still, there is well-founded fear that the security situation in the Republic of Macedonia and the unstable peace that was established after the last year's armed clash caused by the terrorist criminal gangs that are still operating in the Republic of Macedonia could be disrupted if these cases would be tried by the Macedonian courts. Due to this, we believe that the cases should be deferred to the jurisdiction of The Hague Tribunal, due to the temporary absence of legal protection, of the physical integrity of the witnesses and victims in the criminal procedures instigated, were prosecuted [As interpreted] our perpetrators of severe violations of international humanitarian law. The Hague Tribunal has at its disposal legal mechanisms for protection of these people who are frequently victims of kidnapping, torture, or they are witnesses in murders --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Who are in most cases victims of kidnapping, torture, witnesses in other cases. I'm continuing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and with the objective to achieve and secure justice for the victims, to discourage further perpetrations of crimes, to prevent revenge, perpetrators to be convicted and punished, and to contribute towards establishment of a lasting peace at the territory of the Republic of Macedonia. According to the Article 22 from the Statute of The Hague Tribunal that is related to the Court procedure, and according to the Rules 69 and 75 from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Tribunal has the possibility, within a court procedure, to secure protective measures for the victims and witnesses. Macedonian authorities are not objecting to the notion that the supremacy of The Hague Tribunal is established according to the Article 9, paragraph 2, from the Statute, since they believe in the impartiality, honesty, and justice of the Tribunal. But in case that the Prosecution within The Hague Tribunal, or The Hague Tribunal, decide not to defer the five cases, then, according to the Article 9, paragraph 1, from the Statute of the Tribunal, Macedonian judicial institutions, the Public Prosecutor, and the courts, have the legal opportunity and obligation to continue further the investigative procedures and the criminal procedures before the competent national courts, because it is criminal prosecution of perpetrators responsible for severe violations of the international humanitarian law, perpetrators to which the law on amnesty cannot be applied, and the crimes themselves, are not subject to exceeding statute of limitations. Regarding the motion of the Chief Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal that the Chamber decides on deferral of the future investigations as well, we propose to the Court not to accept such motion, for the reasons that the competent law enforcement authorities and bodies, according to the constitution of the Republic of Macedonia, law on public prosecution, law on criminal procedure, and the Criminal Code, have the obligation to undertake identification and prosecution of perpetrators of severe violations of the international humanitarian law. Regarding all future cases of severe violations of the international humanitarian law, discovered, detected, by the Macedonian authorities and perpetrated by the criminal gang NLA, we will continue to inform the Chief Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal, according to the Article 18 from the Statute and the Rule 8 from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of The Hague Tribunal. The methods of deferral of cases, we propose it to be according to the Rule 10 from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, whereupon the Court Chamber of The Hague Tribunal would submit to the competent Macedonian courts an official motion for deferral. Respected President, Honourable Judges of The Hague Tribunal, I hope that you will pay special attention to the contents of the presentation of the Public Prosecutor of the Republic of Macedonia, as well as to the enclosed argumentation and documentation that will be submitted to you after I finish my presentation. Honourable President, Honourable Judges of The Hague Tribunal, honourable colleague Carla Del Ponte, I would like to use this opportunity to thank you for our close cooperation and before the face of the justice should be brought the criminals who have perpetrated severe crimes and have inflicted death and torture to innocent victims. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think the Judges would like to ask both parties some questions. I have -- yes. Yes, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm prepared for the question. But if you allow me, I would have some consideration for what he was telling now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may have the floor, but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'll be very brief. I just wanted to say that we are talking here about five investigations. The Prosecutor of the Republic of Macedonia talked about three investigations and then five investigations. Well, first of all, we never really know how many investigations we should take over or not. Second point: The law on amnesty. We should not forget that between judicial authorities of the Republic of Macedonia and the Macedonian political authorities there is a misunderstanding about the implementation of the law on amnesty. Because the Prosecutor told us we can open investigations, but, according to the law, the competence of the law is related to amnesty on the territory, for crimes committed on the territory, except when the crimes are extremely serious and come under the jurisdiction of the International Tribunal that can open investigations. I take the liberty, Your Honours, of making the proposal of what we find in the judgement of 11th of May, 1995, a decision of that date about Bosnia-Herzegovina. There, in that decision, you can read that the decision of the Trial Chamber [In English] Formally requests the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that its national court defer to the national tribunal all investigations and criminal proceedings, respecting serious violation of humanitarian law are set forth in Article 2(5) of the Statute of the International Tribunal, and here concerning crimes committed during 2001 in Macedonia concerning the population of the city. [Interpretation] So here there is a limitation, a reduction, of the territory in the time period covered. What I'm asking you, therefore, is to adopt the same decision, the decision of 1995, because thus, Your Honours, we will not need again to come back here if there are investigations related to that, and if we find ourselves in the same situation when the Macedonian authorities do not accept our decision but request a formal decision. What I'm doing here is just to prevent that sort of thing happening again. We understand that there is a competition between national and international tribunals, but as for these ongoing investigations, we would like you to give us the possibility of conducting these investigations with the approval of the prosecutor and of the authorities of Macedonia. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I have a question that is addressed to you, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As you put it correctly in your statement that, in my view, in all the international criminal tribunals, including the Nuremberg Tribunal, Tokyo Tribunal, ICTR, as well as ICTY, the investigation and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prosecution of the Prosecutor focus on those who are in the position of authority, that is, the political, military, and the civilian leaders, rather than the minor actors, like the foot soldiers. And in your statement you agreed with that point, but you added: "But we have to start with the crimes committed on the smallest level than to go up to the ladder." I was very much puzzled, you know, by your statement. Would you please elaborate on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can elaborate, but I'm not going to give you the names of my suspects, because for that I would have to ask not only for a closed session, but I would have to ask for an ex parte hearing as well, if I were to give you these names. What I wanted to tell you is that obviously we have some information, some elements, about these crimes having been committed and coming under our jurisdiction. We have opened these investigations. We are currently conducting an exhumation. That's been done, but we don't have the results. We've found a grave. We are currently interviewing witnesses in order to establish that crimes were committed, crimes coming under our competence, our jurisdiction. And whilst interviewing these people and interviewing witnesses of these facts, we are going up the chain of responsibility. We still -- we already have suspects. Our basic investigations, here I'm talking about. But it's true that we do not -- we are not here to conduct investigations on those who actually committed the crimes, but whilst investigating these people, we can identify the responsibility of high-level civil servants, high-level representatives. But currently, Your Honour, we are at a stage where we are collecting evidence on the ground, but we have elements pointing to the responsibility of -- grave responsibility of high-level people. I believe that's all I can say at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. But I also remember that in your statement you said: "At this stage you are not quite sure whether you are going to institute prosecution or indictment," or something like this, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know very well, Your Honour, that we have evidence, but the evidence we have is not sufficient for us to be able to draw up and to issue an indictment. We are working on these investigations, as you know, and we might very well be able to find out the truth. We might be able to collect enough evidence to draw up an indictment, but it's also possible that we won't do that. But in that case, you have the lower-level actors identified, and if that's the case, then we'll transmit the information, the evidence, to national authorities who deal with minor perpetrators. But at the time, currently, we are working in order to establish the responsibility of high-level perpetrators, as is clearly stated in the mandate given to us by the Security Council. However, at this stage of the prosecution, I cannot be 100 per cent certain, and I do not want either to unveil what we are currently doing in detail, but what we need is to have direct access to the territory. We need to feel direct access to the people in order to be able to interview witnesses and in order to be able to complete the investigation. That's why we need to have jurisdiction on crimes committed on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia in 2001, from January. Well, you could limit that. The Prosecutor told us when these crimes, these violations, were committed. January 2001 up until September 2001. If you give us the jurisdiction for that period, even a limited jurisdiction, that's good for us, because that's the period we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Judge El Mahdi, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, I have a number of questions for you in order to gather some information and to increase my knowledge here. Based on this specific case - I'm talking about the two accused who are currently being tried by the local authorities and who are mentioned in your letter of the 26th of June, 2002. So this is very recent. And it seems to me that you left the possibility open for local authorities -- you left them the opportunity, the possibility, to do what they want, i.e. to decide whether these people are suspects, accused -- you did that at the time. But now that they are in the process of being tried, they might be in detention. How do you consider a deferral in that specific case? What I mean is: Are they still going to remain in detention, if they are detained? Because -- and here I will have further questions for the representatives of the Republic of Macedonia, but my question is: What do we do with the accused who are currently in detention?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That's a problem we had previously, because they had 56 or 59 detainees. There was a sort of internal conflict or internal struggle within the Republic of Macedonia about that, because it was said that the law on amnesty made it compulsory for all these people to be freed. If you look at the domestic law on amnesty of Macedonia. But I believe that the prosecutor of Macedonia will be better able to answer your question. Part -- some of them, I think about most of them, were freed. These two, these two detainees we are talking about, were kept in detention, and obviously a clear violation of the law on amnesty, according to some. However, according to the Prosecutor, and we discussed the matter, according to him, or he told me that the judges of the court believe that these two detainees could not benefit from the law on amnesty. But don't ask me why all the others were set free and not these. I just know that two of them were still in detention, and one of them, by the way, is a minor, is under age. Obviously, when we invoke -- I invoke the primacy of the Tribunal, and it's not up to me to make a decision on the domestic jurisdiction, but when you accept the primacy of the Tribunal, either the Republic of Macedonia requests an arrest warrant from us, and if we needed an arrest warrant, we would have asked you to issue an arrest warrant. But I must say that as part of the investigation we are currently conducting, we don't have enough evidence about these two people to ask for an arrest warrant or to establish anything, even if they had asked for that. So the letter you mentioned, it's just a letter where we said: Well, as part of our investigation, we don't have any evidence against these two detainees. It's up to you to make a decision. But they had to make some sort of decision about these two people. Obviously, if I have the primacy, if it is recognised, then either they will transmit additional evidence to us about that, or these people, these two people, will be set free as well. Thus, my letter was written in order to stress the authority of the national jurisdiction about that, about the detention of these two men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: I have another question for you. If I understand very well the law on amnesty does not deal with serious violations, and here we can talk about concurrent jurisdictions between the Tribunal, with the primacy, and national jurisdictions. Yes. Allow me to develop my point. Here we are talking about concurrent jurisdiction, and if I remember well, when the Security Council issued Resolution 827, the four members, the four permanent members of the Security Council issued interpretive statements about that in order to explain what they understood by primacy, primacy, something that is set, that is well known, that has to be accepted by everyone. That's the very sense of international case-law and jurisdiction. I don't want to talk here about primacy. What I want to raise is the issue of concurrent jurisdiction. You know, probably better than myself, that -- you know of a resolution or a decision issued by the Security Council, I believe dating from July 2002, that is binding on you, more than you, when it comes to the way you conduct investigations. This request of yours, when you tell us that you want all investigations to be stopped for one year and you want all investigations to stop about that, don't you think that it, not jeopardises, but don't you think that it sort of challenges the concept of concurrent jurisdiction? Your Honour, I think that the Presiding Judge wanted to tell me something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the question, you know, has been put to you, Madam Prosecutor, and I think we have been warned that, you know, we will have our break in order to change the tapes. So during the break, you may think of your answer, be well prepared, and we'll come back after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we'll resume at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the concurrent jurisdiction, are things clear? I think they are. It's mentioned under Article 9 of the Statute, but it is also quite clear that even if there is concurrent jurisdiction, it is the Tribunal which comes first and which has precedence. You can read this also in the report of the Secretary-General. Therefore, according to the interpretation given to Article 9, there would be concurrent of international jurisdiction and national jurisdiction, but the International Tribunal should come first at any stage of the procedure. Therefore, I wish to state that if we have primacy for this inquiry, investigation, you know that if there are two organs inquiring about the same facts, investigating about the same facts, that may be a source of difficulties in order to get evidence, to gather evidence. This being said, the judicial authority of the Republic of Macedonia may take profit of what will have been gathered in our investigation. But what we request here is to be the first to conduct investigations, because, as you know, we cannot know at this stage of the inquiry where we will get to. So what is being requested now is to be allowed to be the very first to conduct this investigation, while letting the authority benefit, and perhaps even have the responsibility of the trial, thus avoiding any form of collision, any misunderstanding. And let us not forget that our investigation concerns both parties to the conflict, to this armed conflict. It is really necessary to have the same treatment on both sides. I wish to mention the non bis in idem here, this principle which is essentially applicable in the trial, but also for the investigation proper. Your Honours, I would also wish to make another suggestion: Since it is true that our interest concerns these five investigations, this is in fact the centre of what we are interested in, and while less important investigations start, it may happen that it may have an interest for our main investigation. We may have an interest in the smaller investigations in the limited time granted to us. Therefore, my suggestion, if possible, would be to have, if we can now also have the agreement of the Republic of Macedonia, to have referral, deferral, for the five inquiries in question. And for future investigations, we request that the judicial authorities of Macedonia be obliged to inform us, keep us informed, and what we want to avoid is that each time we should come and ask here at a hearing this deferral. So could there be a clause in your decision allowing this, simply on a declaration of the OTP, without having to disturb you on each occasion? So deferral on the five cases, an obligation for the judiciary of Republic of Macedonia to inform us about findings in their investigations or the investigations to come; and thirdly, that declaration of primacy of the Tribunal be valid even when it emanates only from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your very brilliant presentation. I'm concerned about the fate of those who are, for the moment, detained, so I would like to check with the representatives of the Republic whether I have understood fully what was said. They fear that the victims and the witnesses may be threatened, and in this context of uncertainty, do you believe, if you do not intend immediately to direct indictments to determined persons, and having these persons being detained for the moment, if there is deferral towards the Tribunal, normally the bases of their detention will not exist and they will be supposed to have been freed. And do you think there is a risk then, that there is a risk then for them to vanish into thin air, as they say, and that they may be also subjected to threats, or worse? How do you foresee, forecast, the fate of these detained people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said before, the fate of these people detained is not in my hands, not in our hands. Personally, I have jurisdiction to know whether these two accused are also in our inquiry, and they are not because are suspects, are high -- are people who are at the top of the hierarchy. What I do know by our inquiry is that with these two indictees, the charges are not sufficient, in particular one of them, to request here your Chamber an arrest warrant from the Tribunal. So up to now, I can go as far as that, but I cannot go any further. I cannot order the freeing, the release, but this release for me would be automatic from the moment the referral would be formally accepted by the authority, these two people should be released, because it doesn't have competence any more, it doesn't have jurisdiction any more, from a procedural point of view. This is my own opinion, my humble opinion. But this is probably a question which has to be asked from the Prosecutor of Macedonia, because it is a national procedure. All I can do is deal with the procedure of this Tribunal. For me, they are not indicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. With permission of the Presiding Judge, I would like to ask a question for the representatives of the State. If you please, I heard with great interest your presentation, and I would like to be sure that I have understood you well. You've said, inter alia, that there does exist a risk of probable likelihood concerning the victims and the witnesses, of serious crimes which would have been -- come under the jurisdiction of our Tribunal. Now, how do you foresee the case of those who are in detention now? I understand you have detained not only the two, which have been mentioned in the letter of the 26th of June, but also you said that you were detaining also about ten persons, if I understood properly, or perhaps 60 accused, in fact, if I have understood you. So if there were a transfer of jurisdiction to this Tribunal, and while an indictment be drafted against a person in particular, you know, how do you foresee the situation of these accused facing the national jurisdiction during the hinge period, the transition period, if I may say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, respected President and Honourable Judges, first of all I would like to say that if my presentation, I did not manage to explain in its entirety the whole procedure, but I will shortly say here that we are dealing with three cases: The Lipkovo water reserve case, the roadworkers case and the leadership case. As for those suspects, their identities are fully known to us. We are talking now about the two persons in detention. They are related to the Mavovo roadworkers case, and here, in this case, it's not only two persons related, but 23 persons. The question why two persons are in detention, one minor and one of an elderly age is because the rest are in exile and cannot -- and are beyond the law. They cannot be reached by the law. The investigative judge who has issued an order for their arrest, and the police who needs to arrest them and to bring them to the authorities, is not in a position to do so. Therefore, the two persons are in detention, while the rest cannot be reached. As for the two persons who are in detention, they are detained in accordance with the law on criminal procedure, according to which the suspects have limited freedom. In case they are free, whether in Republic of Macedonia or in case you decide that -- for deferral of the case of the roadworkers, the persons, if they are not extradited according to the regulation of The Hague Tribunal. These two persons in relation to the Mavrovo roadworkers case and the rest of the persons, and the environment where this case took place, the embodiment of initials by knife in the backs of the civilian workers, the rapes, et cetera, this all caused a great fear in the whole territory of the Republic of Macedonia. I assume that on the basis of the law, these two detained persons have a limited freedom. However, we deal with a group of perpetrators, altogether 23, and there are the same procedure, according to the Law on Criminal Procedure, is applicable, provided that the other persons are accessible, and if we conduct -- we carry on conducting this investigation, the persons who are in exile should be found in front of our judicial bodies. They avoid to be brought before the justice, and therefore, as a prosecutor, I am proposing to the investigative judge, we have issued an order to detain and arrest them and a detention measure has been pronounced. If the remaining people are to be found, the detention measure will be extended to them as well, and they will be isolated also. Respectable Judges, Honourable Judges, I would like to inform you that when I mentioned 56 persons, they are related to three cases, the NLA leadership, the Mavrovo and the Lipkovo water reserve. Why are these people enjoying their freedom now except for these two detained people? Because the law enforcement bodies cannot access them. If they should be accessible to the law enforcement, the detention measure will be implemented and the court procedure will be instigated before the Macedonian courts. And I would like to inform you on something else regarding the other two cases, that there were mass graves in the village of Neprosteno and the village of Ljuboten. It is the unknown perpetrators, unidentified perpetrators. We have not identified the perpetrators. I would like to ask you that these two cases are investigated by the prosecution before the competent court, the Tetovo court related to the Neprosteno case, where there is a mass grave, and it is a case against an unidentified perpetrator. The second case that my esteemed Prosecutor colleague discussed, the case of the Ljuboten village, the second mass grave where also an exhumation has been performed, I inform you, respecting both Article 18 from the Statute and the Article 8 from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I fully and simultaneously together with us we have conducted investigations related to the exhumations, so that we as authorities, the judicial authorities, made no obstacle to the performance of the investigations by the colleague Prosecutor. Furthermore, as you have heard in my proposal, we are at the disposal to cooperate before it is -- because it is severe crimes and violation of the international humanitarian law that this is all about. I would once again like to stress, regarding the victims and the witnesses, as I mentioned, we have no temporary legal protection, and therefore it could happen that the witnesses and victims as well could be blackmailed or forced -- induced not to appear before the Macedonian courts, and for these reasons in my proposal I explained what could happen in the future, what would be the fate of the victims and the witnesses, and also the cause of the court procedures. For these three cases where we know the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions, if you would allow me. It is not quite clear to me at this very moment. You said that you would agree with the deferral of the three cases you specifically mentioned, that is, the Lipkovo water reserve case, that is the NLA leadership case, and it is the Mavrovo roadworkers case. And then you said about the other two cases, the investigation in respect of mass graves in Neprosteno that perhaps leave that in the hands of the Tetovo court, or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Judge, I would like to inform you that in the case of Neprosteno, that is under the jurisdiction of the Tetovo court and in the case of Ljuboten this is under the Skopje court, so we are active in both cases and both cases are in procedure. We are still investigating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the Prosecutor asks the deferral of these two investigations as well. Would you agree with that or would you oppose again such a deferral?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not opposing to such referral, to those deferrals. We want to obey Article 10 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And on the basis of everything that is presented by my colleague Prosecutor and me as a prosecutor, you, Honourable Judge, decide. Because in our country, according to the positive legal provisions, a formal request from the Court -- from the Tribunal is needed, which we will obey completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, that apart from future cases that have not yet been identified, you do not oppose against the deferral in any of the five cases mentioned by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a second question for you, and that is about the Mavrovo roadworkers case. As you heard, you told us that there are two accused who were due to appear at the 11th of September in court for their trial. Could you inform us about what happened that day? Has the trial taken place or has it been postponed? What happened? What's the actual stage of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Honourable Judges, I want to inform you that the -- that it was the -- the proceeding was procedural delayed. As I am aware, it will continue on the 5th of October. So we lead this process in a regular procedure, respecting the engagements before this Tribunal by the colleague Prosecutor and all -- on that court process we have -- we postponed it because of that. And it has been rescheduled for 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer, and I think that this Court is much obliged that you at least gave us the opportunity first to hear you and not give very hasty decisions. Do I understand you well that if the Chamber would follow the request from the Prosecutor and order the deferral of the Mavrovo roadworkers case, that would include the proceedings against the two accused who appeared for trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, the Mavrovo roadworkers, I again remind you we are talking about 23 suspects that are perpetrators, out of which two are now in detention. It's a legal matter regarding the status of the minor person, because, as far as I know, as far as I know, the provisions of The Hague Tribunal, what status will the minor have. That is one question. And furthermore, what status with the detainees have? Because they are now in detention in Macedonia. With the deferral, in which status they will be deferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I am aware, and I think this Chamber is aware, that the deferral of those who are -- those part of the case that is ready for trial would create all kind of complications. But we have to deal with that. You also told us that these two detained persons have limited freedom. Could you explain what that means, because it was not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The persons that are now in detention by a judge's decision, they are now in a special investigative prison, where there are rules, and it is provided by those rules under which conditions those persons are treated, which is normal. So we are talking about detained persons who have certain rights to be visited, to be seen by others. So this is not -- their contact is not limited with their relatives or with the interested persons, and also with the defence. They are in constant contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I do understand you well, they are, for the full 24 hours a day, in detention, but they have opportunities to have contact with their family and defence counsel. Yes. Thank you for that answer. I also have another question about this Mavrovo workers case. Has the whole file, that means the complete information that you have available, the evidence that you collected during your investigation, has the whole file been at the disposal of the Office of the Prosecution of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my information and to what we have submitted so far, and in accordance with the procedures that have been carried out, the whole evidence material has been submitted, and there is another piece of information. These two persons that are in detention, practically during a procedure, and before an investigative judge, they have been identified as perpetrators in relation to the Mavrovo case, which means that the victims themselves have pointed them out the in a judicial procedure as perpetrators. The victims have identified them as perpetrators of a crime that harms the dignity of the human being, and the minutes, when the identification of these persons was carried out, have also been submitted to my colleague, Madam Carla Del Ponte. This dates back in January 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I have to assume at this very moment that the interpretation or the -- yes, the interpretation of whether there's sufficient evidence to accuse, to indict, and to start a trial, of your authorities is quite different from what the Prosecutor of the Tribunal thinks would be fair and would be right. So we have a difference in assessment of the probative value of the evidence available at this moment. Is that -- am I correct in -- I'm looking both to the Prosecutor of the Tribunal and to you as Macedonian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to inform you, Your Honours, that we are dealing here with two legal systems, one of an international character, and that is you, your Honoured Judges, that acts in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and on the other side it's our system, but we all have the same objective: To bring to justice those who perpetrated crimes, and therefore, every concrete case depends on the evidence material, on the witnesses, which means that the Mavrovo case itself, we estimate it that we can continue with the -- adopt a formal decision to defer the cases before The Hague Tribunal. We will continue to conduct the investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. I have one or two questions for the Prosecutor as well. If I do understand the situation well, you want the investigation, or whatever proceedings are existing of the Mavrovo workers case to be deferred to the Tribunal on the basis of primacy, and at the same time, you do not intend to indict the two accused that are ready to stand trial in Macedonia. For how long would that situation exist? Because when I understood you well, there are two reasons not to indictment them. First of all, because you think that the investigations would not justify an indictment, and the second one is that they are not people of a level of responsibility that would qualify for prosecution at the Tribunal. So for two reasons. You have stressed very much the primacy of the Tribunal, but of course the Rules start to say that there's jurisdiction, both on the national level and for the Tribunal, but the Tribunal can make its primary jurisdiction effective. But in this case, you do not intend to exercise jurisdiction against these two individuals. What, in your view, would have to happen -- I'm putting this question to you because if, for example, these people would be released from detention and would go into exile, then because of the primacy of the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, of which we all know that it will not actually be exercised against these two individuals, would finally frustrate the exercise of national jurisdiction of Macedonia. I'm not talking -- I've got no information about whether your interpretation of the evidentiary material is the correct one or yours, because we haven't seen any evidence. And as I do understand you well, we'll never hear any evidence in relation to these two accused. So it's very difficult for us to assess who is right, the party, the national party who is prosecuting these two individuals or the Prosecutor at the Tribunal, who says that there are no reasonable grounds to prosecute. Could you give us your view, and once the case being deferred -- well, once your investigations have ended, well, let's say, in six months or in one year, that these two individuals would continue to be prosecuted in Macedonia. Because that might be the result. Is that what you would accept? Is that what you seek? And how do you assess the risk of frustrating the national jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I followed attentively your question, and I have to say I agree with what you have said. That is to say, indeed we asked for this primacy, and as I said before, the national authority cannot deal with the case any more. One has to say that it is the Macedonian authority who informed us of this case and who requested us to take it -- as well as the others, three altogether, and we have reviewed in depth this case to see if there was any connection with our own investigations, ongoing investigations, and it was then only that we decided to take it over. We did not forget the fact that two persons were detained. We have particularly reviewed the situation from the criminal point of view of these two persons, and I have to say that all our investigations did not bring us to sufficient evidence or elements to request the Chamber the possibility of having an indictment. It was, I repeat, a very in-depth exercise. I am the Prosecutor, by my mandate, not only with this Tribunal, but I've been a prosecutor for 20 years before that, so before taking the responsibility, responsibility I am taking now, from the moment I obtained primacy and the fact that these two detained are freed, I have to be absolutely sure, and I have asked my investigators to do this research, and I have to say that I cannot today request the arrest of these two. I do not have elements, evidence, of charges against them. The crime for which they are detained is the fact of having interrupted a water supply, cut off the water supply. I think in the village water was not getting to those because the supply had been cut off. And they are part of the group who performed this. But whatever the seriousness of the act of the crime, I have to say my investigators were not in a position -- I must say, I have to tell you, I really monitored this inquiry, and I assure you, I cannot request their arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you? I am a bit surprised by your explanation, because I have very limited information, but it seems that you're referring to a case which interferes with water supply while I was of the opinion that the Mavrovo workers case was the detention and torture of roadworkers rather than those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the accused in the roadworkers case, as far as I understand --

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you -- therefore, if you're talking about the evidence in that case, I'd rather keep it to the case we are talking about and not about evidence in other cases. And I would -- since you told us that there was no evidence sufficient to issue an indictment and to ask the indictment to be confirmed, I just heard from the representatives of the prosecutorial offices in Macedonia that one or perhaps more victims identified the accused as the perpetrators of the detention and torture acts, which in many systems, I would say, would be at least a reason for further thorough investigation. So I'm wondering whether there's -- whether the Prosecution has suspicions about or recognition and the identification of the accused or -- because I'm trying to find out what keeps the international prosecutor and the national prosecutor apart, knowing that usually prosecutors want to prosecute. Could you please explain your position but then in respect of the Mavrovo roadworkers case.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Yes. I mentioned -- I made a mistake. I mentioned that by mistake. I do not know all of the details, but on the fact of recognising, identifying people, we were told that -- the act, of course, has to be repeated. We repeated it. And if I recall properly, in one case there hadn't been no recognition and in another case it wasn't certain, as we demand it to be, the identification. So this is the reason which made us make this decision. Because the hearings or the statements taken by national authorities we have to repeat them. We cannot subsume those which have been made by the national authorities. So that was the result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More or less that the trials here where witnesses have to be appear and where they have to testify in front of the Court and where we cannot rely on former statements, even if these are statements of identification. That's what keeps you apart, did you say, we are afraid that we will not be able to bring any witnesses to do -- to identify the accused here in this court, where perhaps a more civil oriented systems one could easily rely upon earlier statements? Do I understand well that that's what keeps you more or less apart, the system?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: It is one of the elements, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Because that makes it a bit clearer for me. And I'd also like to hear your comment on frustrating the national prosecution, if at least partly for procedural reasons the international prosecution could not be successful. The risk of going into exile and then not appearing for trial in Macedonia, because that's one of your concerns, as far as I understood. Do you feel any responsibility for not frustrating the national jurisdiction where the international jurisdiction cannot be exercised in such a way that it might be successful?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a very good question, but it's a difficult answer for me, because [Interpretation] I have to say that I will take my responsibilities, and in this International Tribunal -- now, if you refer to the case of those who are detained, I have absolutely no hesitation about the fact that the national authority should free them. As a matter of fact, I've discussed the question with the prosecutor during my visit, and I have to say that there was no specific objection to this. But I go as far as that. That is to say, I am looking at my conscience and I can be at peace to say that the two who are in detention now should be provisionally freed. And I even consider, from my own point of view, that it would be an act of justice, without which this would not interfere -- this would not interfere with the national jurisdiction. But from the moment I would be granted primacy, these two persons, I would provisionally free them if it were for me to take a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not just for procedural reasons that where in the Tribunal where the direct presentation of evidence would be required, it's not only for that reason but also because it's your conviction that they're not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. And I would like to add that if, if I had the evidence allowing me to ask, to request their detention, then I would be forced to leave that up to the national authorities because I don't have jurisdiction over low-level officials, because that does not come under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. I could not open a trial here about that, about these people. But I need information about that investigation for my own investigation, and I would confirm that, with regard to these two detainees, even if I was the national prosecutor, I would ask for them to be released, and I'm talking about the merit of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask you a last question. I'm not asking you to go in any detail. If it's your conviction that these two persons should not be prosecuted because they're not guilty, and that's what I hear you saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Until now, because it is a conviction that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the basis of the present evidence of evidential material.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: They cannot be detained in detention now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you have any better candidates for suspicion or indictment? I'm not asking about details, but you can say: I'm not convinced that two people are guilty, and on the basis of the evidence until now, and therefore I'd rather not prosecute them. Another possibility is that you say: The reason why I think they are -- they should not be prosecuted is because they are other people of which I find it far more probable that they would be guilty. Do you have such an alternative? Because if you continue your investigations, it might be that that would result in other suspects. Is there any reason for you to believe that such a result might be achieved in your investigations, or am I asking too much at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: You are asking too much at this moment. But it could be possible. But we must not -- and I will not forget that if Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. during the investigation I would have enough evidence against a low-level or a mid-level perpetrator, I can -- it is in my power to give back a dossier to the national authority to process against these perpetrators, and I'm prepared to do that, and I discussed that with the prosecutor. Because obvious it should be possible. It is not at this moment, but it could be. But despite that, I have no reserve to prepare a dossier with these evidences and to give it back to the national authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I take it that from your discussions with the authorities of Macedonia, that you could not reach, in whatever way, an agreement, or -- because we're sitting here now, and I've heard that you would not oppose against a deferral, but at the same time, you stick to your opinion that a prosecution would be justified of these two individuals where you do not agree. There's no agreement possible, just for, let's say, a delay for further investigation and to reassess the result of such further investigations?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJIKOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, from the first moment of the crisis in the Republic of Macedonia, and during the entire interest of my colleague Prosecutor Madam Carla Del Ponte, we are constantly in cooperation, and as I said, we have an office of The Hague Tribunal in Skopje. I would like to use this opportunity to say once again and to emphasise that we conduct regular court procedure, judicial procedure, for the Mavrovo workers case. We are performing all the evidence, investigation, according to the legislation pending in the Republic of Macedonia. And I would like to emphasise once again regarding the detainees: The suspicion that they are perpetrators and that they should be indicted is based on the identification by the victims before a judge and before a prosecutor. In this occasion I would like to say that before I was a prosecutor general of the Republic of Macedonia, I was a judge in the Republic of Macedonia, so that on behalf of Maja Koneska and my honour, I am not only defending the national law and legislation and the Court procedures, our objective is to bring before the justice the perpetrators, and in this case the evidence has been supported. And I would like to emphasise once again that the evidence has been submitted in January 2002. The complete set of evidence was submitted to The Hague Tribunal, with all our honour, impartiality, and respect to the persons, since the detainees and the suspects in any stage of procedure, be it investigation or indictment or trial phase, they are for us persons respecting the presumption of innocence. But the evidence that have been reached at this stage, as I mentioned, a trial should have been conducted on the 11th of September, but it was postponed for the 5th of October. We have waited, we have considered that this respected Tribunal will discuss the issues, because as a Public Prosecutor and also the presence of the supreme of the Republic of Macedonia, professor Dr. Simeon Gelevski, has informed us that you, the respected Trial Chamber, are requesting presence of the representative of Republic of Macedonia, therefore I elaborated the cases of the NLA leadership, 11 people are suspects, the case of Mavrovo workers, with 23 suspects, and two people out of them are in detention. And regarding the Lipkovo water reserve, there is only one person as a suspect who is inaccessible for the state authorities. I would like to use this opportunity to say that we are conducting the Court procedure regularly and properly and with honesty against all citizens who are mentioned and who are subjects of the Republic of Macedonia. We have no reason to instruct a process with the political background. We have the obligation, I myself as a prosecutor general of the Republic of Macedonia, to respect the constitution and to lead all the evidence in a legal court procedure, and in the case of Mavrovo workers it has been done in such fashion so that there is no suspicion, no doubt in this stage of the procedure, that these two detainees in the case of Mavrovo workers are suspects for perpetration of severe crimes against the international humanitarian law, regardless of the fact that one of them is a minor and the other is of full age, we have the obligation to conduct the procedure. And therefore today before you, Your Honour, respected Honourable Judges, I came on behalf of the Macedonian authorities to explain the cases that are subject interest of The Hague Tribunal, the Prosecutor, Madam Del Ponte, but we are prepared for further cooperation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Judges have exhausted their questions on that subject, and I would like to request to the representative of Macedonia to submit a statement which is not fully delivered today, as well as any attachment it seems necessary for the reference of this Trial Chamber by Friday, which is tomorrow [sic]. In the meantime, this Trial Chamber will deliberate on this matter and we'll render our decisions concerning the deferral of the cases in Macedonia at a later stage. Having said that, we will rise.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.27 p.m.
